tagline: Israel's book of practical wisdom: a father's instruction and hundreds of short sayings on living well in God's world, all rooted in the fear of the LORD.
overview:
Proverbs is a collection of collections. It opens with nine chapters of longer poems in which a father urges his son to choose wisdom over folly, and in which Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman, calls out in the streets and invites the simple to her table. From chapter 10 on, the book becomes mostly single sayings, usually two lines long, on speech, work, money, friendship, anger, family, justice, and the king. It ends with the words of two otherwise unknown sages, Agur and King Lemuel, and a closing poem in praise of a woman of noble character.

The book's motto comes in its first chapter: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). Wisdom in Proverbs is not cleverness or book learning. It is skill in living, the ability to see how God's world actually works and to act in step with it. That skill starts with reverence for God, and it reaches into the most ordinary places: how you talk, how you handle a loan, whether you get out of bed, how you treat a neighbor or a poor man at the gate.

Proverbs matters because most of life is ordinary. The Bible has great stories of exodus and exile, but it also has this book, which assumes that the God who made the world cares how a young man spends his evenings and how a merchant weighs his grain. It trains the reader to notice consequences, to value character over quick gain, and to see daily choices as moral and spiritual choices.
author:
The book names several authors. The heading at 1:1 attributes the proverbs to Solomon son of David, and headings at 10:1 and 25:1 name him again, the second noting that the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied those sayings. Two sections are credited more generally to “the words of the wise” (22:17) and “sayings of the wise” (24:23). Chapter 30 is the words of Agur son of Jakeh, and 31:1-9 the words of King Lemuel, taught him by his mother; neither man appears anywhere else in Scripture, and their home is uncertain. 1 Kings 4 remembers Solomon as a man of great wisdom who composed three thousand proverbs.

Traditional readers have taken Solomon as the source of the book's core, with other material added by later collectors. Many modern scholars think the Solomonic headings honor Solomon as the patron of Israel's wisdom tradition rather than claiming he wrote every line, and they see the book as the product of scribes and teachers over several centuries. Both views agree the book is openly edited: it tells us that Hezekiah's scribes gathered part of it, and it includes material from sages outside Israel's royal court.
date: The book grew over time, and its own headings show that. Solomon reigned in the tenth century BC, and material associated with him could go back to that era. Hezekiah reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC, so the collection in chapters 25 to 29 was copied down at least that late. The final form, including the opening nine chapters and the closing sections, is dated differently by different scholars. Some place the completed book in the late monarchy, before the Babylonian exile; many place its final editing in the Persian period after the exile, in the fifth or fourth century BC. Individual sayings are nearly impossible to date, since proverbs circulate orally for generations before anyone writes them down.
setting:
Wisdom literature was an international genre in the ancient Near East. Egyptian scribes produced books of instruction in which a father or official teaches his son how to succeed and behave rightly, and Mesopotamian texts collected proverbs and advice as well. The closest known parallel to any part of Proverbs is the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a work usually dated to Egypt's New Kingdom or the centuries just after it (roughly 1300 to 1000 BC, with some scholars placing it somewhat later) and first published by modern scholars in the 1920s, whose content closely resembles Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22 at several points. Proverbs 22:20 speaks of “thirty sayings”, and Amenemope is arranged in thirty chapters, though the Hebrew word behind “thirty” is uncertain and many translations adopt that reading partly because of the Egyptian parallel. Most scholars conclude that Israel's sages knew and adapted this Egyptian work, reshaping its advice under the fear of the LORD.

Inside Israel, proverbs would have been taught in the home, where the book pictures father and mother instructing their children, and likely also among royal scribes and counselors who served the king. The world the book assumes is a small agricultural and commercial society: fields and harvests, city gates where elders judged cases, markets with weights and measures, loans secured by pledges, and a king whose justice set the tone for the land.
purpose: The prologue (1:2-6) states the aim: to give wisdom, discipline, and insight; to teach righteousness, justice, and fairness; to make the simple prudent and the young discerning; and to add learning even to the wise. The first readers were young men being formed for adult life, household, trade, and public service, and the opening chapters address a son directly. But the book also expects the mature to keep learning, and its sayings apply to anyone who has to decide how to speak, spend, work, and treat others. Its deepest purpose is to show that ordinary life belongs to God and that walking in his ways is the path of life.
story: Proverbs doesn't advance the Bible's plot the way Genesis or Kings does, but it is anchored in that story. It is tied to Solomon, the son of David, whose reign in 1 Kings 3 and 4 opens with a prayer for wisdom and a reputation for it that reached the nations, and whose later life shows how a wise man can still turn to folly. It assumes the covenant God of Israel, called by his name the LORD, and it echoes the law's call to bind God's words on the heart (Deuteronomy 6). Alongside Job and Ecclesiastes, it forms the Old Testament's wisdom writings: Proverbs states how life ordinarily works under God, and Job and Ecclesiastes press on the cases where it doesn't seem to. In the Hebrew Bible it sits in the third division, the Writings; in Christian Bibles it follows Psalms.
christ:
The New Testament quotes Proverbs several times. Hebrews 12 applies Proverbs 3:11-12 on the LORD's discipline to Christians who suffer, and James 4 and 1 Peter 5 both use the thought of Proverbs 3:34 that God gives grace to the humble. Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30) and says that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). Jesus himself said that one greater than Solomon had come (Matthew 12:42).

The portrait of Wisdom in Proverbs 8, present with God before creation and rejoicing in his work, shaped how the New Testament speaks of Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17), though the chapter itself is a poetic personification, not a prophecy. Christians see in Jesus the one who lived the life Proverbs describes perfectly, and who is himself the wisdom the book's father urges his son to seek.
reading:
Read Proverbs as proverbs. A proverb is a compressed observation about how life usually goes under God, not a promise or a guarantee for every case. “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (10:4) is true as a pattern, and the book knows it has exceptions: it speaks of the poor who are oppressed and of wicked men who prosper for a time. The clearest signal is 26:4-5, where two proverbs placed side by side give opposite advice about answering a fool. Wisdom lies in knowing which one fits the moment. The same applies to sayings like 22:6 on training a child: they describe the normal fruit of faithful parenting, not a contract that makes parents solely responsible for a grown child's choices.

Watch for the two paths and the two women, Wisdom and Folly, that frame the book's opening; for the recurring figures of the simple, the fool, the mocker, the sluggard, and the righteous; and for parallelism, where the second line of a saying repeats, contrasts with, or extends the first. Read the sayings slowly and a few at a time. Many readers take one chapter a day, which fits a book of thirty-one chapters.

structure.title: A father's instruction and Wisdom's call
structure.summary: A prologue stating the book's purpose, then a series of longer poems in which a father urges his son toward wisdom and away from violent men and the adulterous woman, with speeches by Wisdom herself, including her place at creation in chapter 8.

structure.title: The proverbs of Solomon
structure.summary: The largest collection: several hundred mostly two-line sayings, many built on the contrast between the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish, covering speech, work, wealth, family, and the king.

structure.title: The words of the wise
structure.summary: Two shorter collections of longer sayings, the first closely related to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, with advice on the poor, rulers, drunkenness, and laziness.

structure.title: Proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
structure.summary: A second Solomonic collection gathered in the days of King Hezekiah, rich in comparisons from nature and daily life and in counsel about kings and fools.

structure.title: The words of Agur and Lemuel
structure.summary: Agur's humble confession and his numerical sayings, followed by a queen mother's counsel to her son the king on wine, women, and justice for the poor.

structure.title: The woman of noble character
structure.summary: An acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praising a capable woman who fears the LORD, closing the book as it began, with wisdom embodied.

themes.title: The fear of the LORD
themes.body: The book's foundation, stated at 1:7 and again at 9:10, is reverent awe toward the LORD, the God of Israel. This fear isn't terror but a settled recognition of who God is, which shows itself in humility, obedience, and turning from evil. Wisdom in Proverbs is never simply shrewdness; it grows from this root, and the book returns to it at its close in the praise of a woman who fears the LORD.

themes.title: Two ways
themes.body: Proverbs pictures life as a road with two paths: the way of wisdom and righteousness, which leads to life, and the way of folly and wickedness, which leads to death. Choices that look small, a companion, a loan, a glance, a lie, set a person on one road or the other. The book trains the reader to see where a path ends before stepping onto it.

themes.title: Wisdom personified
themes.body: In chapters 1, 8, and 9, wisdom speaks as a woman who calls in public places, offers life and favor, and was present with God when he made the world. Her rival, Folly, also calls to passers-by. The personification makes the choice concrete and personal: to choose wisdom is to accept an invitation to a relationship, not only to master a set of rules.

themes.title: Words and speech
themes.body: Few subjects get more attention in Proverbs than the tongue. The book contrasts honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip and discretion, flattery and faithful rebuke. Words build up or tear down a household and a city, and restraint in speech is repeatedly treated as a mark of wisdom.

themes.title: Work, wealth, and the poor
themes.body: Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard, but it also warns against trusting riches, against dishonest gain, and against oppressing the poor. It says that the LORD defends the needy and that kindness to the poor is lending to God. Wealth is a real good in the book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.

keyChapters.why: The prologue states the book's purpose and its motto, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, and Wisdom first raises her voice in the streets.
The call to trust in the LORD with all your heart, and the teaching on the LORD's discipline that Hebrews 12 applies to Christian suffering.
Wisdom's great speech, including her presence with God before and during creation, a passage central to later Jewish and Christian reflection on the Word and on Christ.
The two banquets of Wisdom and Folly bring the opening section to its decisive choice.
The start of the Solomonic sayings shows the book's typical form: short, contrasting two-line proverbs.
Contains the much-quoted saying on training a child and the beginning of the words of the wise, with their links to Egyptian instruction.
Lemuel's mother's counsel on justice for the poor and the acrostic poem of the woman of noble character that closes the book.

parts.body:
Proverbs is the twentieth book of the Bible. It has thirty-one chapters, and it is Israel's book of practical wisdom: how to live well, day by day, in the world God made.

It opens with nine chapters of longer poems. A father speaks to his son and urges him to choose wisdom over folly. Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman, calls out in the streets and invites the simple to her table. Then, from chapter 10, the book becomes mostly short sayings, usually two lines long, about speech, work, money, friendship, anger, family, justice and the king. It ends with the words of two otherwise unknown sages, Agur and King Lemuel, and a poem in praise of a woman of strength.

The book's motto comes in its first chapter: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline” (1:7). Wisdom in Proverbs is not cleverness or book learning. It is skill in living: seeing how God's world actually works, and acting in step with it. That skill starts with reverence for God, and it reaches into the most ordinary places, how a person talks, handles a loan, gets out of bed, or treats a poor man at the gate.

Most of life is ordinary. The Bible has great stories of exodus and exile, and it also has this book, which assumes that the God who made the world cares how a young man spends his evenings and how a merchant weighs his grain.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Proverbs belongs to the Bible's wisdom books, with Job and Ecclesiastes, and with the Psalms and the Song of Songs close by. In Christian Bibles it comes right after the Psalms. In the Hebrew Bible it stands in the third part, the Writings.

It does not move the Bible's story forward the way Genesis or Kings does, but it is tied to that story. Its heading names Solomon son of David, whose reign opens in 1 Kings 3 and 4 with a prayer for wisdom and a name for it that spread among the nations. ‘Solomon composed three thousand proverbs’ (1 Kings 4:32). The same books go on to tell how a wise king could still turn to folly.

Proverbs assumes the covenant God of Israel, called by his name, the LORD. It echoes the law's call to keep God's words close to the heart (Deuteronomy 6). And it speaks to every human being as a creature in a world God made, which is why it can learn even from the wisdom of other nations.

The three wisdom books argue with one another, and the Bible keeps the argument. Proverbs says how life ordinarily goes under God. Job and Ecclesiastes press on the cases where it does not seem to.

The book names several authors. The heading at 1:1 credits the proverbs to Solomon, and headings at 10:1 and 25:1 name him again. The second of these adds that these are proverbs ‘which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah’ (25:1). Two sections are credited more broadly to the words of the wise (22:17; 24:23). Chapter 30 is the words of Agur son of Jakeh, and 31:1-9 the words of King Lemuel, taught him by his mother. Neither man appears anywhere else in the Bible, and where they came from is uncertain.

Readers understand the headings in two main ways. Traditional readers take Solomon as the source of the book's core, with other material added by later collectors, as the headings themselves say. Many modern scholars think the Solomon headings honor him as the patron of Israel's wisdom rather than claiming he wrote every line, and they see the book as the work of scribes and teachers over several centuries. Both views agree that the book was openly gathered and edited. These notes take no side.

The book grew over time, and its headings show it. Solomon reigned in the tenth century BC, about 970 to 931 BC on the reckoning the site's guide to the kings follows, so some sayings could go back to his day. Hezekiah reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC, so chapters 25 to 29 were copied down at least that late. The finished book is dated differently by different scholars. Some place it in the last years of the kings, before the exile. Many place its final editing after the exile, in the fifth or fourth century BC, and many think chapters 1 to 9 were among the last parts to be written. Single sayings are almost impossible to date, since proverbs pass from mouth to mouth for generations before anyone writes them down.

Israel's wisdom belonged to a wider conversation, and the Bible says so itself. Solomon's wisdom is compared with ‘all the wisdom of Egypt’ (1 Kings 4:30). Proverbs includes the sayings of Agur and Lemuel, who may not have been Israelites at all.

Egypt and Mesopotamia had long traditions of instruction, in which a father or a king passes advice to a son. The best-known parallel to Proverbs is an Egyptian work, the Instruction of Amenemope, usually dated about 1300 to 1075 BC. An Egyptian official wrote it for his son in thirty chapters. In 1924 the Egyptologist Adolf Erman showed that the section of Proverbs beginning at 22:17 closely parallels it in content and sometimes in wording, especially in 22:17 to 23:11: listening carefully, not robbing the poor, avoiding the hot-tempered man, not moving the ancient boundary stone, and the skilled worker who will stand before kings.

Proverbs 22:20 asks, “Have I not written for you thirty sayings about counsel and knowledge,” but the Hebrew word behind ‘thirty’ is uncertain. Many translations read it that way partly because of Amenemope's thirty chapters, and others have read it as ‘formerly’ or ‘excellent things’.

Most scholars conclude that Israel's sages knew Amenemope's work and adapted it. Some conservative scholars have argued instead that both drew on a common source. Either way, the change is what stands out. The Israelite version sets the borrowed advice under trust in the LORD: “So that your trust may be in the LORD” (22:19). And it gives the poor a defender: ‘for the LORD will take up their case’ (22:23). Wisdom from beyond Israel was brought under the rule of Israel's God.

Proverbs is a collection of collections, marked off by its own headings.

Chapters 1 to 9 are longer poems. A prologue (1:1-7) states the book's purpose and its motto. Then a father speaks to his son in a series of talks, each opening with the father's call to his son, and Wisdom speaks for herself in chapters 1, 8 and 9. These chapters are the doorway. They give the frame for reading the short sayings that follow.

The proverbs of Solomon (10:1 to 22:16) are the largest collection, several hundred two-line sayings with little obvious order, though scholars have found clusters linked by shared words and themes. The scholar Patrick Skehan noted that there are 375 of them, the number the letters of Solomon's name add up to in Hebrew. Whether that is design or coincidence is debated.

Then come the words of the wise (22:17 to 24:22), the part related to Amenemope, and a short appendix (24:23-34). Chapters 25 to 29 are a second collection of Solomon's sayings, copied by Hezekiah's men, rich in pictures from farm and weather and in counsel about kings and fools. The words of Agur (chapter 30) include his sayings that count things up, three and then four. The words of Lemuel (31:1-9) are a queen mother's advice to her son. The book closes with a poem of twenty-two verses (31:10-31), each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in praise of a woman of strength.

The son addressed in the book reflects the setting of family and court teaching. It has long been read as addressed to every reader, man or woman, and the book ends by praising a woman as the picture of wisdom lived out.

parts.h: What a proverb is, and is not
parts.body:
A proverb is a short saying that catches something generally true about life. The Hebrew word, mashal, covers proverbs, comparisons, riddles and parables: ways of setting two things side by side so that one throws light on the other. Proverbs are short on purpose. Each one catches a single angle. Wisdom lies in knowing which one fits the moment.

The book makes the point itself. It sets two opposite sayings next to each other: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him” (26:4), and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes” (26:5). The ancient rabbis noticed it. The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) records a debate over whether Proverbs should be withdrawn because of it, and the answer given was that the two sayings apply to different situations. Both are true. The wise person sees which one the moment needs.

So proverbs are not promises or guarantees. “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it” (22:6) says how things usually go and urges parents to take training seriously. It does not promise that every child of faithful parents will believe, and reading it as a guarantee has laid heavy and undeserved guilt on many parents. The same is true of the sayings that tie hard work to wealth: “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (10:4). Proverbs knows the world is not so simple. It says that injustice can sweep away the poor man's crop (13:23), and it puts doing right above having much: “Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with turmoil” (15:16).

Proverbs also sets human planning under God's rule: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (16:33). The German scholar Klaus Koch argued in 1955 that the Old Testament sees deeds as carrying their results inside them, more than God handing out rewards from outside. Others think he drew the line too sharply, since Proverbs also speaks of the LORD repaying. Either way, the book describes the moral grain of a world God made. It is not a vending machine.

The whole book stands on one foundation. It is said at the start, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7), again at the end of the opening poems, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding” (9:10), and once more in the last chapter, where ‘a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised’ (31:30).

The fear of the LORD is not terror. It is reverence, awe and trust toward God that shows itself in obedience: a settled recognition that God is God, and that a person is not. It is the beginning, the first step and the starting point. Proverbs never treats wisdom as mere shrewdness. A clever person who does not fear God is still, in the book's word, a fool.

That is why the book can sound so practical and still be about God on every page. Honest scales, careful words and hard work are not a separate, secular part of life. ‘The eyes of the LORD are in every place’, as one saying puts it (15:3), and ordinary life belongs to him.

parts.h: A father's voice, and two invitations
parts.body:
Chapters 1 to 9 are built as a father's talks to his son. The mother's teaching stands beside the father's: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother” (1:8). Egyptian teaching texts used the same form, a father speaking to his son. Proverbs keeps it, and aims not only at success but at righteousness, justice and fairness before the LORD.

The son hears two kinds of voices. One is the gang that promises easy money through violence (1:10-19). Another is the woman who belongs to another man and offers stolen pleasure (2:16-19; 5; 6:20-35; 7). Against them stands Wisdom, who calls in the busiest places of the city, ‘Wisdom calls out in the street, she lifts her voice in the square’ (1:20), and who promises life to anyone who will listen.

The talks are frank about sex and its power. They warn against adultery in vivid terms, and they also praise faithful married love as a gift: ‘rejoice in the wife of your youth’ (5:18). The warning is written to a young man, and it puts the weight of responsibility on him: he is the one who must keep his path far from her door (5:8). The danger it names, sweet words with hidden costs that wreck a marriage and a life, can tempt anyone, and many readers apply the warning in both directions. The book speaks just as hard words about violent and deceitful men, and it does not teach contempt for women. Its other great figure, after all, is Wisdom herself.

The opening poems end with two invitations (chapter 9). Wisdom has built her house and set her table. Folly calls from her doorway too. Every reader has to decide whose meal to eat.

In chapter 8 Wisdom speaks at length. She was there before the world began: “The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old” (8:22). When God set the heavens in place and marked out the sea, she was beside him: “Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence” (8:30).

Wisdom here is a personification: a quality of God given a voice and presented as a person, a common way of speaking in Hebrew poetry. The poem says that the world was made wisely, and so wisdom fits the grain of things. To find her is to find life (8:35).

The chapter had a long later history. Jewish writers after the Old Testament, such as Ben Sira, identified wisdom with the law of Moses. The New Testament speaks of Christ in language close to this chapter: the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3), the one in whom all things were created and hold together (Colossians 1:15-17). The chapter shaped that language. But the chapter itself is a poetic personification, not a prophecy, and these notes read it that way.

In the fourth century AD verse 22 became a battleground. The Greek translation has Wisdom say that the Lord ‘created’ her, and Arius and his followers took that as proof that the Son of God was a created being. The Hebrew verb, qanah, more often means to acquire or possess, and translations still differ. Athanasius and other defenders of the faith confessed at Nicaea in AD 325 answered that the poem is about God's wisdom and should not be pressed into a statement about the Son's origin. The church's confession that the Son is eternal and not made rests on the New Testament's own direct teaching (John 1:1; Colossians 1:15-20; Hebrews 1), not on reading every detail of Proverbs 8 as a description of him.

parts.h: The sayings: words, work, money and friends
parts.body:
From chapter 10 the book changes pace. Most sayings are two lines long, and the second line repeats, contrasts with or carries forward the first. Read a few at a time, slowly, and turn each one over.

Some subjects come back again and again. Speech is the first of them: honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip and silence. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (15:1). Words can build a household or burn it down.

Work is another. The slacker, who will not get out of bed and always has an excuse, is one of the book's sharpest and funniest portraits (6:6-11; 24:30-34; 26:13-16). Money is a third. Proverbs calls wealth a real good, but always a lesser one than wisdom, honesty and a good name, and it warns against dishonest scales, hasty riches and the loan secured for a stranger.

Friendship runs through the book too. ‘A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity’ (17:17). ‘As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another’ (27:17). So do anger, pride, envy, drink and the king, whose justice sets the tone for a whole land.

Over all of it stand the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool. The book's cast becomes familiar: the simple, who are naive and can go either way; the fool, who is settled in folly; the mocker, who sneers at correction; and the righteous, whose path ‘is like the first gleam of dawn’ (4:18). The reader is meant to see himself in more than one of them.

parts.h: The poor, and the God who made them
parts.body:
Proverbs has a great deal to say about the poor, and it says it in God's name. “The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all” (22:2). “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (14:31). Kindness to the poor is even called a loan to the LORD (19:17).

Some sayings link laziness with want, and readers sometimes take them to mean that the poor have earned their poverty. That is not the book's view. It knows that hunger can come from injustice (13:23) and that the poor are often shunned while the rich have many friends (14:20; 19:4), and it reports these things as a sad fact of life, not as something to approve. Its warnings about laziness speak to the reader about the reader's own habits. They never give anyone a reason to look down on someone who is poor.

The book's last word to a king is about the poor. Lemuel's mother tells him: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed” (31:8). A ruler's strength is measured by how he defends those who cannot defend themselves.

Proverbs speaks often about raising children, and it is honest about how much a home shapes a life. A few of its sayings about correction need to be read with great care.

Several sayings speak of the rod: “He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently” (13:24), with 22:15, 23:13-14 and 29:15. Faithful Christian parents read them in two main ways. Many take them as instruction to parents, endorsing measured physical discipline of young children, given calmly and in love, never in anger, and always aimed at the child's good. Others read the rod as a picture of correction in general, since the same book speaks of ‘a rod for the backs of fools’ (26:3), and hold that Proverbs describes the methods of its own culture rather than a technique for every age. They point to the New Testament's word to fathers: “do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21). This question divides faithful parents without dividing anyone from Christ, and these notes take no side.

On the most important things both sides agree. The target of these sayings is the parent who never corrects at all, which the book calls a failure of love. Correction given in anger, or that injures a child, is not discipline at all. No reading of these verses gives anyone a warrant to harm a child. They permit no injury and no abuse, which the whole Bible condemns.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Proverbs also has sayings about a quarrelsome wife (19:13; 21:9). They are not a comment on women in general: the very next saying after 19:13 calls a prudent wife a gift from the LORD (19:14). They are a frank picture of a home without peace, and the book warns just as plainly about the angry man (22:24; 29:22). They are not a license to despise anyone, and they do not tell anyone to stay where they are in danger.

parts.h: Agur, Lemuel, and the woman of strength
parts.body:
The last two chapters bring new voices. Agur begins humbly, ‘I am weary, O God, and worn out’ (30:1), confesses how little he knows, and asks God for a modest life: ‘Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion’ (30:8). His sayings count things up, three things and four, and look closely at creatures such as the ant and the rock badger. Lemuel's mother warns her son against wasting his strength on women and wine, and charges him to speak for the poor.

The book ends with a poem in praise of a woman of strength. ‘A wife of noble character, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies’ (31:10). The word behind ‘noble character’, chayil, is often used of strength, valor and even an army. She buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades cloth, provides for her household and opens her hand to the poor. Her husband and children praise her.

Readers take the poem in several ways: as a portrait of an ideal wife, as Wisdom from chapters 1 to 9 now living in a real household, or as both. In Jewish homes it is traditionally sung by husbands to their wives at the Sabbath meal, as praise rather than a checklist.

Whatever reading one takes, the poem is praise, not a standard any woman must meet. Its twenty-two verses gather many excellences into one picture, and turning it into a burden would misuse it. Its heart is verse 30: “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.” The fear of the LORD, where the book began, is open to every believer, married or single, woman or man.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Proverbs
parts.body:
The New Testament quotes Proverbs several times. Hebrews 12:5-6 takes up 3:11-12 on the LORD's discipline and applies it to believers who are suffering: “For the Lord disciplines the one He loves” (Hebrews 12:6). James and Peter both quote 3:34 in its Greek form: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Paul quotes 25:21-22, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Romans 12:20). Peter quotes 11:31 in its Greek form, “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” (1 Peter 4:18), and 2 Peter uses 26:11: “A dog returns to its vomit” (2 Peter 2:22). When Peter writes that ‘love covers over a multitude of sins’ (1 Peter 4:8), he echoes 10:12.

The New Testament also speaks of Christ in the language of wisdom. Paul calls Christ ‘the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 1:24), and says that in him ‘are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge’ (Colossians 2:3). Jesus said of himself, ‘now One greater than Solomon is here’ (Matthew 12:42). And, as the part on chapter 8 says above, the New Testament's language about Christ as the one through whom all things were made draws on the picture of Wisdom at creation, though the chapter itself is poetry about God's wisdom and not a prophecy.

These notes keep to the lines the New Testament draws, and do not add others.

Read Proverbs as proverbs. A proverb is a short observation about how life usually goes under God, not a promise for every case and not a law for every situation. When two sayings seem to pull against each other, as 26:4 and 26:5 do, the book is asking for judgment, not offering a contradiction.

Read it slowly. Many readers take one chapter a day, which fits a book of thirty-one chapters. Take a few sayings at a time, and ask which one fits the day in front of you.

Watch for the two paths and the two women of the opening chapters, for the cast of the simple, the fool, the mocker, the slacker and the righteous, and for the way each saying's second line answers the first.

Read it beside Job and Ecclesiastes. Proverbs without them can turn into a formula that blames the suffering and the poor. With them, it is what it was meant to be: a patient training in the fear of the LORD, for the ordinary days that make up most of a life.

hard.line: Wisdom laughs at the calamity of those who refused her. A prophet's warning in poetry, spoken while there is still time to turn.
Long life and full barns for those who trust the LORD: the usual fruit of wisdom, not a guarantee against loss.
The forbidden woman. The warning is written to a son, but the danger it names belongs to both sexes, and the book teaches no contempt for women.
Getting free from a pledge for another's debt: wise caution about rash promises, not a ban on helping anyone.
‘The LORD created me’. Poetry about God's wisdom, and a battleground in the fourth century over whether the Son was created.
Idle hands make one poor. A pattern for the reader's own habits, never a verdict that the poor deserve their poverty (13:23).
The rod and the son. Faithful parents read it in two ways; neither reading gives anyone a warrant to harm a child.
The LORD made even the wicked for the day of disaster: nothing escapes his purpose, not that he creates anyone in order to destroy them.
A bribe works like a charm in the eyes of the one who gives it. An observation, condemned elsewhere in the book (17:23).
A quarrelsome wife. A picture of a home full of strife, not a license to despise anyone or a reason to stay in danger.
Train up a child. How things usually go, not a promise that blames parents whose grown children walk away.
Strike him with a rod. Read with 13:24: correction instead of neglect, in readings that differ, and never a warrant for harm.
Do not answer a fool, and answer a fool: two true sayings set side by side, and wisdom knows which one the moment needs.
Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint. Vision here is God's word to his people, not a plan for the future.
What is the name of his Son? Read as Israel, as an ironic challenge, or as a glimpse that later Scripture takes up.
The woman of noble character: praise, not a standard every woman must meet. Its heart is the fear of the LORD (31:30).

words.line: A proverb, comparison or parable. It sets one thing beside another so that a pattern in life becomes visible (1:1).
Fear. The fear of the LORD is reverence, awe and trust that shows itself in obedience, the beginning of knowledge (1:7; 9:10).
Wisdom: the skill of a craftsman, the insight of a wise adviser, and above all the art of living rightly in God's world (1:2).
The simple: naive, inexperienced, open like a door anyone can walk through. Not yet a fool, and able to go either way (1:4, 22).
The fool: not someone lacking intelligence but someone settled in folly, who will not learn (1:22; 26:1-12).
To mock or scoff. The mocker sneers at correction and so cannot be taught (9:7-8).
The slacker or sluggard, who will not start, will not finish, and always has an excuse (6:6-11; 26:13-16).
Discipline or instruction: teaching and correction together. For Proverbs, being teachable and being correctable are one virtue (1:2; 12:1).
Rod, staff or scepter: a shepherd's staff, a ruler's scepter, an instrument of correction. Proverbs uses it of fools as well as sons (13:24; 26:3).
The heart: the center of thought, will and desire, not only of feeling. “Guard your heart with all diligence” (4:23).
Loving devotion, steadfast love, kindness, or loyalty. Bound with faithfulness around the neck (3:3).
Righteous: a person in right relationship with God and neighbor, set against the wicked throughout the sayings (10:1-32).
To acquire, buy or possess, and in a few places to create. ‘Get wisdom’ (4:5), and the much-debated verb of 8:22.
Something detestable or an abomination to the LORD, such as dishonest scales and haughty eyes (6:16; 11:1).
Strength, capability, wealth or valor. The woman of noble character is an eshet chayil, a woman of strength (31:10).

timeline.what: The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope is written, an official's advice to his son in thirty chapters, close to Proverbs 22:17 to 23:11.
Solomon reigns. He asks God for wisdom, and he composes three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 3; 4:32).
Some sayings may go back to Solomon's day. Proverbs pass from mouth to mouth for generations before they are written.
Hezekiah reigns in Judah. His men copy further proverbs of Solomon, now chapters 25 to 29 (25:1).

timeline.when: Before the exile, on one view
timeline.what: Some scholars place the finished book in the last years of the kings of Judah.

timeline.when: The 400s or 300s BC, on another view
timeline.what: Many place the book's final editing after the exile, in the Persian period, often with chapters 1 to 9 among the last parts.
An Aramaic papyrus of the Words of Ahiqar is copied at Elephantine in Egypt: a sage's sayings and story, with parallels to proverbs on discipline and speech.
The letter of James, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it, quotes Proverbs 3:34 (James 4:6). Others date the letter later.
Paul writes Romans and quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 (Romans 12:20).
Hebrews is written, most often dated in the 60s, and applies Proverbs 3:11-12 to suffering believers (Hebrews 12:5-6).
1 Peter, if Peter wrote it, quotes Proverbs 3:34 and 11:31 (1 Peter 5:5; 4:18). Others date the letter later.
The Council of Nicaea confesses the Son begotten, not made, after a long argument in which Proverbs 8:22 was a key text.
Adolf Erman shows that Proverbs 22:17 to 23:11 closely parallels the Instruction of Amenemope.

map.title: The one place on this map

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Proverbs names no place in the land. Its headings name two kings who reigned here: Solomon son of David (1:1) and Hezekiah king of Judah, whose men copied Solomon's proverbs (25:1).

teaching.mapNote: Proverbs names no place in the land, so the map shows only Jerusalem, where the kings named in its headings reigned. Egypt, named once for its colored linen (7:16), lies beyond the edge of this map. Massa (30:1; 31:1), if it is a place at all, is not placed in this site's records and is left off. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
